title: Chapter Fifty-Seven: Mingshe
bio: “Mingshe” — in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, the Central Mountains, in the waters of Mount Xian there are many mingshe; shaped like a snake with four wings, its cry is like the ringing of a stone chime, and where it appears the town suffers a great drought. Truly, a snake's body with four wings, a cry like a chiming stone — some sounds fall silent for years yet never truly vanish; once they sound again, the old storms follow in their wake, and things long thought to be over come pressing close once more.
paragraphs: Xi'an, the High-Tech Zone. At ten thirty at night, few people were left in Xinghuan's offices.

Wu Peng sat in his own office, two phones in front of him. One was the work phone he used every day; the other was a spare kept only for project communications. He had already listened to the afternoon call three times over. The recording was not long — a little over four minutes. The first half was his exchange with Zhang Hailu about the non-compete clause; the second half held the unexpected find.

When Zhang Hailu had asked Diao Kexin for instructions on the phone, he thought he had cut the speakerphone. In fact he had only suspended it; the line stayed open. The few words Diao Kexin spoke next were caught, clear as day, by the recording function on Wu Peng's other phone.
Wu Peng played the recording again.
“It wasn't me — it's probably Mr. Zheng! What am I supposed to say, Director Diao?”
Then Diao Kexin's voice: “Tell him it was Old Zheng. You can offer evidence — drive a wedge between them!”
Wu Peng paused the playback. He leaned back in his chair, turning the pen in his fingers.

The value of that exchange went far beyond what he had expected. For one thing, the mere fact that Zhang Hailu and Diao Kexin were handling the call together confirmed where he had gone — Yuanwang, with Diao Kexin, just as suspected. Add the hole with Yuanwang's finance chief now sitting on the board, and the substantive chain of evidence for the non-compete was complete.

On the other hand, if Zhang Hailu had merely denied handling those accounts, it could still be read as a departing employee protecting himself under company investigation. But Diao Kexin's interference changed the nature of the whole thing. She not only knew he was under investigation; she had openly urged him to push the blame onto Zheng Zhiyong. The question now was whether to disclose the recording to Zheng Zhiyong — because that one instinctive jab would only fan the war smouldering between Diao Kexin and him.
Wu Peng picked up his phone, called Wu You and briefly walked him through it; then he played the last few lines of the recording for him.
Wu You listened, and did not give an opinion at once.
“You kept the original?”
“Yes. Both phones have it.”
“Don't forward it yet. Don't tell anyone. Don't use it to provoke anyone. Keep the original file, the call log, the timestamps. Don't even give it to the company's legal department.”
Wu Peng said, “Uncle, this recording proves directly that Zhang Hailu has joined Diao Kexin's team. Wouldn't it be valuable to hand it to Legal and protect our rights?”
“What's your goal? Do you want Zhang Hailu back at Xinghuan, or do you want him away from Diao Kexin? Our aim isn't to sue for damages under the non-compete, is it?” Wu You's tone stayed calm.
“Uncle, given the situation as it stands, is Zhang Hailu's return still an option?” Wu Peng asked.
“From where I sit, if we win the Xi'an bid, we'll still be short of people. If Zhang Hailu comes back, what stands in his way?”
“One, rebuilding his trust with Xinghuan. Two, the real pressure of looking after his family.”
On the other end of the line Wu You nodded, pleased. “Go on, Wu Peng. Keep talking.”

Wu Peng paused a moment, then went on. “We've used the non-compete to talk to him this once. If he doesn't know we hold real evidence, the trust isn't completely torn. And the simpler thing — solving the real pressure on him and his team to care for their families — that's easy enough: we open an office in Xiangcheng, or even in his old hometown of Xiangtan, so he can care for his family far more directly than from an office an hour's drive from home. Uncle, if we land Xi'an, absorbing the cost of one additional technical office shouldn't be much of a problem.”

“You're right, Wu Peng, but you've missed one key thing. In today's call, he may not know you recorded it, and he may not know you already know he's with Diao Kexin — but in his own heart, his relationship with Zheng Zhiyong is already broken. There's a very dark place in human nature: a man can never again trust the person he has betrayed, whether or not that person still trusts him.”
Wu Peng chewed over his uncle's words. He didn't quite follow. “Why?”
Wu You smiled faintly. “That's human nature.”
“So you mean the only person he can still work with now is Diao Kexin?”

Wu You said, “I mean, he may not have stopped trusting Xinghuan. But after today's call, having chosen self-preservation, he'll have one more reservation about Mr. Zheng. As for Xinghuan, as long as we don't let on that we know he's gone to Yuanwang, and stop pressing the point, he can go on trusting us. Or — here's what I think — if he has some fear of the non-compete, and the Xi'an result is still unknown, or Yuanwang simply fails to win the bid, he won't go on working with Yuanwang either. Technical people are simple. If you live by your skills, you don't have to take risks. You can eat anywhere.”
“Uncle, if Mr. Zheng really did hold back some benefit on the fan lights project, how do you see it?”

“That fan lights order was a civilian product line. It was really Zheng Zhiyong cashing in his own technology — the company spent almost nothing on it. That he put the proceeds into the company back then was something I genuinely admired. It showed his sense of responsibility as a leader. Or rather, at that stage he understood what that income was worth in leverage — helping the company win larger orders later. For that stage, the order had done its job. Old Zheng's contribution was complete.”
Wu Peng thought for a moment. “Uncle — you don't want to pursue it?”

“No. I don't want to pursue it. But the matter can serve as Zhang Hailu's pledge of loyalty for coming back, and as one card in building deeper trust with Zheng Zhiyong. The man now is not the man who threw himself into the work when he first arrived. Something has changed.”
“Technically speaking, Mr. Zheng is a man worth keeping. I think he's someone Xinghuan wants to hold on to,” Wu Peng said.

“You're right, Wu Peng. Old Zheng's strengths have always been technology and fighting hard battles. But these past months, looking at the financial and operational reports, and at how you've maintained customer relationships in sales — I've seen it. You have your own strengths.”
Wu Peng said, “So if Mr. Zheng and I work well together, wouldn't that be a better choice for Xinghuan's future?”

Wu You said, “That depends on how Zheng Zhiyong sees his own role, and on what he wants. These past two years I've genuinely tried to groom him into a better CEO. But this loss of the team may have hit him hard. In a sense, it's not a question of whether I want him to stay — it's whether he wants to.”

Wu Peng said, “Uncle, the 10% management stake and the 6% GP of the partnership are both in Mr. Zheng's name now. With real equity and future dividends like those, he should be satisfied, shouldn't he?”

Wu You said, “In the last stage, as a technical partner, Mr. Zheng was up to the mark — he deserved those returns. Looking ahead, though, what matters more than our judgement is his own wish, his own will to do this. Put another way, I don't prejudice the case. Two years of running Xinghuan have given Zheng Zhiyong a certain foundation. Do you see what I mean?”
Wu Peng nodded.
Wu You said, “When do you expect the result on Xi'an?”

Wu Peng said, “We'll submit all the supplementary material before the lunar New Year. Then, once work resumes after the spring festival, we should hear something in about two weeks. Dr. Xiao has brought in two engineers she knows, and they've been fitting in well with the existing team. As far as I can tell, the material is coming together smoothly.”

Wu You said, “You and Shasha did a great job pulling Dr. Xiao back into the project. Judging by her actual performance, Xiao Jing's technical ability seems no weaker than Zheng Zhiyong's — wouldn't you say?”
Wu Peng said, “My sense is that Mr. Zheng's strengths are motors, hardware, systems and supply-chain management. Dr. Xiao is exceptional in algorithms. Their strengths complement each other.”
Wu You said, “Good, Wu Peng. What we've said today stays between the two of us.”
After he hung up, Wu Peng glanced again at the computer screen.

It struck him suddenly that this might be the biggest difference between Wu You and himself. Given a recording, his first thought was what it could prove; Wu You's first thought was what it could change. He saw events; Wu You saw people. He saw the present; Wu You saw past, present and future. His uncle had brought up Xiao Jing today — was he trying to make him think more deeply about the company's future staffing? What if Old Zheng chose to stay? And if Old Zheng chose to leave, how would Xinghuan's technical team make a smooth transition? The thoughts rose in Wu Peng's mind, one after another.

He did not notice that his way of thinking was quietly changing. He was moving from the operator's habit of getting things done toward a manager's habit of thinking about the survival of the enterprise.

Meanwhile, Zheng Zhiyong was still alone in his hotel room in Xiangcheng. At that moment he missed Xi'an more than he could say. For two years the fourth-floor apartment at Xinghuan had been a safe, independent harbour for him — a temporary home, decent and settled. The company whose equity he truly held, that small white building, held the team he had built with his own hands, the friendship of fighting side by side, and moments full of warmth. Xiangcheng, by contrast, held nothing but strange memories — betrayal and regret written into every corner of the city.

Zhang Hailu had not called again. The way he had hurried off that day, with the embarrassment of a man seen through — two years of hard-won friendship had seemed to dissolve in the winter wind, right then.

Diao Kexin — that woman. Zhu Yiwen had steadied her waist and helped her into the Maybach. Her goal in life had always been to be the boss's woman; that was why she kept finding herself a boss and becoming his mistress, smooth as ever.

Xiaoya had been back in Chengdu for a week. These past days she had not contacted him on her own, nor posted a single moment online. It was as if she had never appeared in Zheng Zhiyong's world at all.
And what had his own wholehearted love for her been? And what was it — after losing her — to seek the solace of love in a younger woman who looked like her?
He opened the computer and logged into an encrypted hard drive. Inside was a folder labelled with just two words: Diao Kexin.
The folder held photos, chat logs, some old project files, and a recording. He had kept that recording for many years.

It dated from the time when he and Diao Kexin were closest. One night, deep in conversation, she had been drinking and in high spirits, and told him about a stretch of her life at the Sixth Academy — about the powerful patron she had there, and the details of how she had climbed, seduced, paid huge bribes, the amounts, and the way the handovers were done. As she spoke, there was little shame in her voice; if anything, a recognition of her own ability. To her, it was simply one way of surviving in the business world.

Old Zheng had shown nothing outwardly. But inwardly he was startled, and without thinking he hit the record button, capturing at their most intimate moment a piece of leverage he could use against her.
That leverage was like a knife hidden at the very back of a drawer.
Old Zheng closed his eyes.
He thought of years ago, when the two of them were still together.

Back then Diao Kexin was far less composed than she was now. A project's outcome could make her nervous; a leader's slow reply could set her anxious; and late at night she would hold him and ask whether she was a terrible woman.
Old Zheng had once believed he understood her better than anyone in the world. He knew her ambition, knew her fragility, knew how high a price she would pay to get the things she wanted.

He had also believed that over the past few years he had matured, had come to know himself better. But at this moment he was lost. He did not know whether he should take this knife and drive it into the woman who had hurt him before, and was now hurting him again, hard.

He lit a cigarette. 10% of the management equity, a 500,000 yuan year-end bonus — proof that his two years of running the company had been recognised. Yet after everything that had happened lately, he found himself suddenly at a loss about his own life. Not long ago those things had been what he dreamed of. Now he was no longer so sure what it was he wanted.

He glanced at the recording on the screen. It could drag Diao Kexin out of the fix she was in — having slipped free of detention — and sink her deeper: no longer a passive recipient of orders or an unaware bystander, but the mastermind behind the seduction and the bribes. This knife could damn her beyond redemption. It could also reverse, in an instant, the situation at the bid opening after the New Year: if a company in the running loses its actual controller, Xinghuan's odds rise sharply.
It came to him suddenly: the knife was in his own hand.
But the things Diao Kexin spoke of in that recording, serious breaches of rules and discipline though they might be — what role had he played? He was not merely a listener.

He had been her lover, the person closest to her. If he turned words spoken in the most intimate of moments into a weapon against her, would he not become a man odious to look at — the very kind of man he had once hated most in his life?
Old Zheng flicked the ash into the ashtray. For the first time, he felt he did not want to use this card he had hidden for so many years. Not at all.
Just then, his phone rang.
It was Lu You, who had not been in touch for ages.
“Mr. Zheng, where have you been lately?”
“I'm in Xiangcheng on business.”

“What a coincidence. I was calling because I want to get the old friends together before the year is out — I was going to say, if you're in Xi'an, let's have dinner next week. I never thought you'd be in Xiangcheng. I'm here too. Forget next week — let's just meet here.”
“All right. See you tomorrow. Send me a time and place that suits you.”

“Hey, I've got a younger cousin who teaches at a university here in Xiangcheng. I've asked him to dinner tomorrow evening, so we old friends could meet tomorrow at noon, how's that? I'll send you the hotel address in a bit; we'll find somewhere close by.”

At noon the next day the two met as agreed at a Hunan restaurant. Over the past years Lu You had been a very special figure in Zheng Zhiyong's life. Often Zheng could not only take his advice, but when he was at a loss would actively want to seek him out and unburden himself. So Lu You's call the night before had felt to Zheng Zhiyong like nothing short of telepathy. Once they met, after three beers, Old Zheng poured out the whole story — how he and Diao Kexin were rivals again, how she had poached the team he had spent two years building. But the other matters, those fleeting romances, he left out entirely.
When Lu You had heard him out, he could not help saying, “Diao Kexin is a formidable woman. The strength of her purpose — she's no ordinary person.”
Old Zheng said, “Only yesterday did I understand that I have the power to take revenge on her — even to push her into an abyss with no way back. But the truth is, I don't want to do it at all.”

Lu You said, “Because that's your nature. The greatest value of building a business may lie not only in success, but in coming to know yourself — in tempering your humanity through the process. And besides, the gains and losses of the world shouldn't be the measure of whether a life succeeds or fails.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “I've decided not to win that way. I'll still beat her.”
Lu You nodded. “By the way, where did you say this Diao Kexin was from?”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “She came out of the mountains of southeastern Guizhou. I even went back to her home with her once.”

Lu You nodded, and could not help thinking: the young cousin on his mother's side he was to meet that evening was from southeastern Guizhou too. His young aunt had married there years before and run a timber business there. It struck him as quite a coincidence, but he said nothing of it.

Lu You went on, “A few people leaving the team — you can build it up again. But more important than rushing to rebuild is your own thinking. Another year is nearly gone. How does your boss Wu You see your work? If he's dissatisfied, do you have any plans?”

Zheng Zhiyong said, “True, a few important people have left, but the company is past the survival stage; the continuing business earns enough each year to support the team. Still, you're right — I've been doing some thinking of my own lately. I'm beginning to feel that being a professional manager isn't really where I belong. Sooner or later I may have to consider working for myself. But right now we're at the tensest point of the bid, still pulling the documents together. I have to help the company and my boss win this fight.”
Lu You said, “Nobody can fault Old Zheng's sense of duty and responsibility. So how's your love life lately? Have things eased up with your wife?”

Zheng Zhiyong shook his head and sighed. “I can't even get to see her. But the pain has taught me one thing: if a middle-aged man hasn't sorted out how to survive, hasn't got a career of his own, then all this talk about love is bullshit — meaningless.”
Lu You chuckled. “So Mr. Zheng has passed the test of the heart. When a man passes that test, his career is ready to take off. Come on — here's to an early takeoff.”
The two clinked glasses.

When the meal ended, Lu You set out to call on a contact at the local university — and as it happened, his younger cousin taught at the same school, so he had arranged to meet the cousin and his family for dinner that evening. The cousin had a very unusual name, given him by Lu You's dear young aunt: it was meant to say “live long,” and in Chinese it was Li Fulang. The cousin had divorced seven or eight years earlier; he had heard that around then an accident had injured his leg and left him limping for good. But work had gone smoothly, and with his parents looking after him devotedly, his spirits had slowly recovered. He remarried five years later, and recently a little boy had been born. That evening Lu You was going on behalf of his mother's side of the family to congratulate the household on its new addition, and planned to hand over a fat red envelope.
And after his meeting with Lu You, Old Zheng's spirits lifted considerably; he made ready to return to Xi'an.
